title: How the Spanish Inquisition Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Spanish Inquisition, starting with the broader medieval Inquisition founded under Pope Gregory IX in 1231 and staffed by the Dominican Order. They cover how it operated (secret accusers, no lawyers, judge-decided trials, torture sanctioned by Pope Innocent IV, a forty-day grace period for confession, forced confession twice), the targeting of converted Jews (conversos/conversos) and Moriscos, Ferdinand and Isabella's motives of religious unity, power, and confiscated property, Tomás de Torquemada's role, the strappado and rack, auto de fé ceremonies, executions handed to secular authorities, the spread of inquisitions to Portugal, Goa, Mexico, and the Roman Inquisition (Galileo), the last Spanish executions in 1826 and 1834, the 1858 Edgardo Mortara case, and the debate over the death toll after the Vatican's secret archives were opened. The episode closes with a long listener mail and gift thank-you segment and a sponsor read.

segments.title: Opening banter and setup
segments.summary: Hosts joke about name pronunciations, Monty Python and Mel Brooks Inquisition sketches, and introduce the topic of the Spanish Inquisition as misunderstood and contested.

segments.title: What the Inquisition was and who it targeted
segments.summary: The Inquisition was a church court where judges decided guilt, accusers were anonymous, and defendants had no lawyer. Heresy was defined broadly and included converts, witchcraft, bigamy and sodomy, with much of the targeting based on faith.

segments.title: Origins: medieval Inquisition and Spanish Inquisition
segments.summary: The papal Inquisition began in 1231 under Pope Gregory IX, staffed by the Dominican Order, and targeted Christian dissidents. Ferdinand and Isabella later launched the Spanish Inquisition to unify Catholic Spain, with motives tied to power and money through confiscated land.

segments.title: Persecution of Jews, Moriscos, and converts
segments.summary: Converted Jews (conversos) and Muslims (Moriscos) were suspected of secretly practicing their old faiths. The 1492 Alhambra Decree banished Jews from Spain, and the suspicion of crypto Jews triggered the Spanish Inquisition. Inquisitions also spread to Granada, Portuguese India (Goa), and Mexico.

segments.title: Other inquisitions and Galileo
segments.summary: Portugal and Rome also ran inquisitions. The Roman Inquisition tried Galileo, who was placed under house arrest and reportedly received a papal pension.

segments.title: Trial process and grace period
segments.summary: Trials had no lawyers, unknown charges, and forced testimony. Inquisitors gave a forty-day grace period for voluntary confession. Confessions had to be repeated outside torture, and penance could include land loss, fines, labor, or exile.

segments.title: Torquemada, torture, and methods
segments.summary: Torquemada, the Grand Inquisitor, is seen as the face of the Inquisition and reportedly set rules limiting torture. Pope Innocent IV had authorized torture. The strappado and rack are described, along with the physical damage they caused.

segments.title: Auto de fe, executions, and the end of the Inquisition
segments.summary: The auto de fe was a public religious procession where sentences were announced. Executions were handled by secular authorities, often by burning. The last Spanish executions were in 1826 and 1834, and the 1858 Mortara case is mentioned.

segments.title: Death toll debate and Vatican archives
segments.summary: The Vatican opened its secret archives under Pope John Paul II, who apologized. A 2004 report put executions at roughly one percent of about 125,000 trials. Hosts note that figures vary and that Spain's state often carried out executions.
